reading.title: The Press in the Harbor Alley
reading.purpose: Follow an apprentice printer watching her coastal town stand up to an unfair governor.
paras: In the coastal town of Marlow, sixteen-year-old Clara wiped ink from her thumbs as her uncle locked the print shop's wooden shutters. For two winters, the royal governor had ruled through sheer tyranny, wielding cruel, unlimited power while raising harbor taxes without a single town vote. Whenever merchants voiced open dissent—publicly disagreeing with his decrees—soldiers marched down the pier to fine their shops.

The governor tried hardest to control the printed word. His officers arrived every Tuesday to censor the town gazette, crossing out any line that questioned harbor tolls. When Clara's uncle printed a pamphlet anyway, guards threatened to persecute the whole print guild, targeting them unfairly week after week until they shut their doors. Yet attempts to suppress the news only made neighbors trade handwritten copies faster.

By spring, a retired shipwright named Maren became the town's boldest activist, organizing meetings in the candlelit fish market. First, dockworkers called a strike, halting all unloading until wages matched the soaring bread prices. Next, families joined a peaceful boycott, refusing to buy imported tea or cloth from the governor's own warehouse. Even neighboring ports placed a trade sanction on the governor's cargo ships, penalizing his fleet until he listened.

Four weeks later, the harbor stood silent except for crying gulls. With empty ledgers and stalled ships, the governor finally signed a charter agreeing to abolish the unfair harbor toll permanently. That evening, Clara unlocked the shutters and inked a fresh headline—the first page in two years printed without a single crossed-out line.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "boycott" most nearly means
choices: a secret newspaper printed behind locked wooden shutters
a group's refusal to buy certain goods as a peaceful protest
a sudden storm that blocks cargo ships from entering a bay
a fine charged by soldiers against merchants on the pier
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines boycott directly as "refusing to buy imported tea or cloth from the governor's own warehouse."

qs.q: Which sentence shows that the governor's crackdown on news failed to stop information from spreading?
choices: The governor tried hardest to control the printed word.
His officers arrived every Tuesday to censor the town gazette, crossing out any line that questioned harbor tolls.
When Clara's uncle printed a pamphlet anyway, guards threatened to persecute the whole print guild, targeting them unfairly week after week until they shut their doors.
Yet attempts to suppress the news only made neighbors trade handwritten copies faster.
qs.why: This sentence directly states that trying to suppress the news backfired and made neighbors share handwritten copies even faster.

ev.text: Yet attempts to suppress the news only made neighbors trade handwritten copies faster.

qs.q: Why did the governor finally agree to end the harbor toll?
choices: The combined strike, boycott, and port penalties stalled his trade and emptied his ledgers.
Clara's uncle promised to print only flattering stories about the governor's warehouse.
Winter storms destroyed the fish market before Maren could organize a second meeting.
The dockworkers decided to pay the higher taxes in exchange for cheaper imported cloth.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 notes "empty ledgers and stalled ships" after the strike, boycott, and trade sanction forced the governor to sign the charter.

qs.q: What is the central theme of this story?
choices: Printing gazettes by hand is much faster than using a coastal town's wooden press.
Coordinated, peaceful resistance from workers, families, and neighbors can overturn unfair power.
Harbor taxes are always necessary to pay for soldiers and candlelit fish markets.
Apprentices should stay out of public debates until they own their own print shops.
qs.why: Through dissent, a strike, a boycott, and neighboring sanctions, the town peacefully compels the governor to abolish the unjust toll.

clues.text: crossing out any line that questioned harbor tolls
refusing to buy imported tea or cloth from the governor's own warehouse

reading.retellFrame: When the governor tried to ___ the town, residents worked together using ___ until he agreed to abolish the toll.
